Because experimental dataset discrimination can reflect acquisition-specific cues, we develop controlled synthetic and experimental evaluations and find that structural discrimination benefits from dense spatial features. We introduce the EMber family of vision transformers, pre-trained on >50 million experimental particle images from 214 EMPIAR datasets together with simulated projections from 268,000 molecular assemblies. EMber improves upon existing methods at conformational and compositional discrimination by 14.85 and 14.26 percentage points, estimates conformational populations to within 1.59pp error with a linear probe, and produces particle assignments yielding reference-quality reconstructions in fewer epochs. We demonstrate how to learn representations that capture biological information for use across multiple cryo-EM inverse problems.

papers.title: Solvability of complex Hessian equations corresponding to right-Noetherian polynomials
papers.abstract: On compact Hermitian manifolds, we establish a framework using radial normalization for the solvability of complex Hessian equation in form type, corresponding to right-Noetherian polynomials whose coefficients may not be constant functions. The solvability of a radial normalized equation is characterized by the existence of a C-subsolution at radial slope, which extends the results of Guo-Song to this setting.

papers.title: alkhder at AlexandriaX-2026: Context-Aware English-to-Dialectal Arabic Dialogue Translation with QLoRA-Fine-Tuned NileChat-3B
papers.abstract: This paper describes team Alkhder's submission to Subtask 1 of the AlexandriaX-2026 shared task, which asks systems to translate English dialogue turns into thirteen Arabic dialects. We fine-tune NileChat-3B-Base with QLoRA on the Alexandria parallel dialogue corpus, training one set of adapter weights for all dialects. Each turn is translated conditioned on the target country and dialect, the domain, the participant roles, the speaker-addressee gender direction, and the preceding dialogue context. At inference, conversations are translated autoregressively and the model is fed its own previous outputs back as context without using any gold target-side test information. Under the constrained track, using only Alexandria data, it trains in about one hour and translates the private test set in under two hours. The system reaches a country-macro-averaged spBLEU of 20.36 and chrF++ of 36.64 on both tracks.

papers.title: Literal Lock-In: How Test Language Shifts Literal Attraction in Typed Decision Models on Bengali Idioms
papers.abstract: Decision models, non-generative scorers that report a probability over caller-supplied options and emit no text, are increasingly deployed as routers, classifiers and guardrails. Because they generate nothing, rationales and chain-of-thought do not apply. We audit three: an encoder scorer, a decoder scorer and a closed API, entirely through interventions on their input, using expert-annotated Bengali idioms carrying a gold figurative and a gold literal gloss. Dropping an idiom's own literal gloss into the option list draws every arm toward it, taking 65% to 96% of each arm's remaining Bengali errors. A model-by-language matrix over one shared item set shows how far this depends on the test language: every arm is 1.9 to 6.4 times more captured in Bengali than in English on the same paired entries, the commercial model's apparent resistance is a property of its test language, and capability does not order the failure. Calibration degrades in all three arms, and on the open arms confidence inverts, so gating on it is worse than gating at random. On a semantics-free option list, where accuracy is at chance, the best-calibrated arm still reports mean confidence 0.82. Code and data: https://github.com/sakhadib/literal-lock-in.

papers.title: Nonrelativistic quantum theory of non-dipole effects in a multielectron atom: radiation transition operator
papers.abstract: In the work of Hopersky A.N. et al., arXiv: 2609.33494v1 [physics. atom-ph] in the Loudon integral representation, the general analytical structure of the complete operator of a multipole radiation transition taking into account non-dipole effects for a multielectron atom is established. In this Letter this structure is converted to the sum only for all multipoles.

papers.title: ForTress: Bringing Assurance and Determinism for LLM-Driven Fortran-to-Python Translation
papers.abstract: Modernizing mature scientific software from Fortran to Python can improve accessibility and integration with modern computing tools, but manual rewriting is expensive. Large language models (LLMs) make translation more practical, yet generated code can pass regression tests while violating source-language semantics, and contextual corrections may not persist across subsequent translations. We present ForTress, which solidifies recurring LLM translation decisions into guarded executable rules for deterministic reuse and provides semantic assurance for a non-trivial subset of these rules. Its LLM-assisted auditing process expresses universally quantified preservation obligations over mechanized Fortran and Python semantics in Lean. Human experts review semantic fidelity and correspondence with production rules, and Lean's kernel checks proofs and refutations under explicit assumptions. These audit records expose the conditions either supporting correctness or identifying failure cases. We evaluate ForTress on 17 benchmarks from 15 scientific software spanning diverse domains. The translated programs achieve bitwise-identical with native Fortran on all evaluated tests under the recorded execution and initialization configurations. Against these software, ForTress accumulates 193 executable rules and 188 audit records, of which 121 have checked soundness proofs, including 31 established after counterexample-guided refinement. Cross-software reuse exceeds 90% for 14 of the 15 software. Even with additional assurance and determinism, the LLM usage cost is 44.2% lower than direct LLM translation.

papers.title: Pearl-Chat: Engineering a native Luganda language model from first principles in JAX and Flax NNX
papers.abstract: Autoregressive foundation language models predominantly target high-resource Indo-European languages, imposing computational and morphological penalties on under-represented African languages. Generic multilingual tokenizers routinely exceed fertility rates of 3.2 tokens per word on agglutinative Bantu languages, degrading context efficiency and inflating latency. We present Pearl-Chat, an 8,473,122-parameter ($\sim$8.5M) causal decoder-only transformer engineered for Luganda (Oluganda, ISO 639-2: lg), a low-resource Niger-Congo Bantu language spoken by over 10 million people in East Africa. Built from first mathematical principles in JAX and Flax NNX, Pearl-Chat uses explicit functional state decomposition (nnx.split and nnx.merge), deterministic resumable data streaming via Google Grain, and SPMD tensor parallelism using jax.sharding.Mesh. We introduce a byte-level byte-pair encoding (BPE) subword tokenizer trained from scratch on curated Luganda corpora ($V = 8,192$), achieving 4.88 characters per token compression and 1.60 tokens per word fertility, a two-fold compression improvement over LLaMA-3 (128K) and Gemma (256K). The model is trained with a two-stage curriculum: Stage 1 pre-training on 59,501 sequences across parallel, biblical, encyclopedic, and journalistic corpora, and Stage 2 instruction fine-tuning on 510 dialogues with assistant-only loss masking. Across 4,000 optimization steps, validation cross-entropy loss drops monotonically from 9.4695 (perplexity: 12,958.98) to 0.1818 (perplexity: 1.20), a decrease of 9.2877 nats. On a three-tier held-out diagnostic benchmark, Pearl-Chat achieves 0.9792 ROUGE-L and 0.9405 BLEU while maintaining concordial agreement across Bantu noun classes. We provide a Python Server-Sent Events (SSE) streaming runtime and open-source all weights, tokenizers, and code.

papers.title: Constraints on Decaying Dark Matter with $B=1$ from Fermi-LAT
papers.abstract: We investigate the gamma ray signatures of fermionic dark matter that carries one unit of baryon number and decays into three quarks. We compute the expected prompt and secondary gamma-ray spectra for a representative range of final state flavor combinations. By comparing these spectra to Fermi-LAT measurements of the isotropic gamma-ray background, we derive exclusion limits on the lifetime. We observe that depending on the dark matter mass and the flavor of the final state, the lifetime bounds on decays of $B=1$ dark matter can differ by up to a factor of two from those on decays of $B=0$ dark matter. Furthermore, light-quark final states generally yield stronger bounds at lower masses, whereas heavy-quark final states can yield comparable or stronger bounds at masses of tens of TeV and above.

papers.title: Thermo-viscous feedback in heat transport through fracture-matrix systems with finite thermal capacity
papers.abstract: In geothermal systems, injected fluid flows along preferential fracture pathways and exchanges heat with matrix blocks. Reduced models often neglect temperature-dependent viscosity and assume unlimited matrix storage, although the thermal capacity accessible to the flow is finite. This work analyzes thermo-viscous feedback in a planar fracture-matrix system where viscosity controls discharge through the integrated hydraulic resistance, while finite capacity enters through an effective single-timescale memory fixed by initial uptake and total capacity. The reduced model gives parsimonious semi-analytical predictions with physically based parameters, verified against the nonlinear solution. A perturbation hierarchy separates matrix storage from the hydraulic response it induces, while an exponential velocity reconstruction preserves the exact terminal discharge and bounds front-moment errors within the front-moment limit model. At fixed pressure difference, heating accelerates and broadens the front, whereas cooling delays and sharpens it. The terminal discharge depends only on the endpoint viscosity ratio, while matrix uptake, storage and contrast determine its approach time. At fixed rate, viscosity alters only the pressure drop, not the thermal response. Finite thickness controls the transition to capacity-limited equilibration, and strong matrix uptake collapses the isoviscous response onto a two-variable similarity surface.

papers.title: Resonant pair production and flat band melting in a driven Rydberg chain
papers.abstract: We study a Rydberg chain subjected to a two-tone periodic drive of the detuning $Δ(t)$ and Rabi frequency $Ω(t)$ at frequencies $ω_1$ and $ω_2=νω_1$ respectively with $ν\in \mathbf{Z}$. In the strong Rydberg blockade limit, such a system reduces to the PXP model and exhibits exact Floquet flat band. Here we determine, using a time-dependent Schrieffer-Wolff transformation, the domain of validity of such PXP dynamics once the blockade-violating processes are taken into account. We study the melting of such flat bands in the presence of strong, but finite, blockade strength. Using Floquet perturbation theory (FPT), we identify two mechanisms for such melting; the first occurs due to the presence of many-body resonances involving resonant production of nearest-neighbor Rydberg excitation pairs while the second involves virtual processes that access intermediate states with such pairs. Our analytical FPT results match with those obtained using exact diagonalization on a finite chain. We study the dynamics for $|{\rm vac}\rangle$ (Fock state with no Rydberg excitation), $|{\mathbb {Z}}_2\rangle$, and $|{\mathbb {Z}}_3\rangle$ (Fock states with Rydberg excitations on alternate and every third site respectively) initial states. We find that $|{\rm vac}\rangle$ shows exceptional stability against resonant pair formation while $|{\mathbb {Z}}_3\rangle$ exhibits flat band melting via virtual processes away from the direct resonances. We find oscillatory dynamics with large time period for the $|{\mathbb {Z}}_2\rangle$ initial state and the presence of Floquet scars that have large overlap with $|{\mathbb {Z}}_3\rangle$ state; these phenomena occur due to processes that are absent in the PXP limit. We propose measurement of nearest neighbor pair correlation functions using Rydberg atom quantum simulator platforms as an accessible experimental probe for these effects.

papers.title: The Singular Structure of Rapidity Distributions for Color-Singlet Production at N3LO
papers.abstract: We determine the universal singular structure of rapidity distributions for color-singlet production in hadron collisions through next-to-next-to-next-to-leading order (N3LO) in QCD. Our result captures the full singular contributions as either partonic momentum fraction approaches one, including the delta-function terms, while retaining the exact dependence on the other. The essential new ingredient is the complete calculation of the three-loop quark and gluon rapidity beam-function matching kernels. Our calculation is based on the strict collinear expansion of the partonic cross sections for Higgs boson and Drell-Yan production. We represent our results in terms of generalized polylogarithms as well as numerical series expansions. The resulting N3LO partonic coefficient functions apply to arbitrary color-singlet production processes with the process dependence entering through the hard function, which encodes the virtual corrections to the Born process.

papers.title: A Unified Framework to Prioritize Population and Precision Health Research
papers.abstract: Background: In an era of precision health, researchers must prioritize among research directions addressing different sources of uncertainty and variation. Research may reduce parameter uncertainty (e.g., improve average treatment effect estimates) or explore unexplained individual-level heterogeneity (e.g., identify new biomarkers). Existing frameworks evaluate these directions separately, limiting direct comparisons. We develop a unified framework for jointly estimating the value of resolving parameter uncertainty and unexplained heterogeneity. Methods: Our framework comprises six uncertainty states combining available parameter and unexplained heterogeneity information, extending the Value of Unexplained Heterogeneity framework. We define the value of a research direction as the difference in value between two states. We formalize counterfactual outcomes across interventions to estimate value and suggest ways to reduce computational burden. We illustrate the framework using a three-option microsimulation model. Results: The framework enables direct comparison of research value across sources of uncertainty and variation. In the illustrative example, exploring unexplained heterogeneity had the greatest value. Comparing the value of resolving unexplained heterogeneity across individual-level outcome components (e.g., health states, costs, and side effects) indicated little value in personalizing interventions based on whether patients entered the sicker state. Conclusion: Our framework enables direct, quantitative comparisons of the value of different research priorities and identifies the one with the greatest potential to improve population-level cost-effectiveness. It serves as a practical tool for performing research prioritization in the era of precision health.

papers.title: D-Composer: Language Modeling for Simultaneous Drum Transcription and Sound Event Decomposition
papers.abstract: Drum beats are often conceptualized and produced as arrangements of repeated single-drum sound events or one-shots. Drum Analysis-by-Synthesis (AbS) models combine this structural assumption with reconstruction-based training to perform MIR tasks such as drum transcription, drum source separation, and one-shot extraction, offering a flexible alternative to more traditional task-specific supervision. However, leading AbS approaches struggle to generalize to a broad range of drum timbres (e.g., electronic drum kits), rely on high-quality paired audio-transcription training data, and do not model intra-class timbral variation within a single arrangement (e.g., multiple kick sounds). To overcome these limitations, we propose D-Composer, an autoregressive language modeling framework that decomposes drum recordings into labeled sound events and their onset times. In drum transcription and one-shot extraction tasks, D-Composer performs comparably to or better than a state-of-the-art AbS system and task-specific baselines while generalizing to a broader range of drum timbres. Our results demonstrate that when equipped with abundant synthetic data and compact acoustic token representations, language modeling provides a simple recipe for unifying transcription and sound event decomposition.

papers.title: Failure of direct finiteness for group algebras in every odd characteristic
papers.abstract: For every odd prime $p$, we construct a finitely presented group $G_p$ and elements $a,b,c\in\mathbb{F}_p[G_p]$ such that $ab=1$, $ac=0$, and $c\ne0$. Thus $\mathbb{F}_p[G_p]$, and the group algebra over every field of characteristic $p$, fails to be directly finite. The construction combines a single exceptional self-product pair with signed bipartite cancellation. New integer matching data realize the exceptional self-intersection while retaining a strict squared-word decay estimate. We verify the adaptations needed for the earlier bounded-path and planar-localization arguments. A minimal disk picture protects the identity coefficient of $c$, so the proof does not require torsion-freeness.

papers.title: FlashControl: One-Step Controllable Generator via Distillation-Friendly Single-Stream Teachers
papers.abstract: Diffusion models have become a leading approach in visual generative modeling, particularly effective in text-to-image and controllable generation. Their main drawback is slow inference as it requires many sampling steps. While recent distillation methods enable one-step text-to-image generation, extending these techniques to controllable generation is still challenging. Existing controllable models, such as ControlNet, rely on dual-branch design that make distillation difficult. In this work, we adopt a simpler strategy. Instead of adding extra conditional branches, we finetune a selected subset of layers in the original text-to-image diffusion model to directly enable controllable generation. This results in DeltaControl, a single-flow, multi-step diffusion model capable of supporting spatial-condition generation while matching the performance of dual-branch approaches. Building on this teacher model, we further apply step-distillation to obtain FlashControl, a one-step model capable of spatial controllable generation with a single forward pass.

papers.title: Are Large Reasoning Models Good Everyday Reasoners? A Comparison with Non-Reasoning Models on Logical Reasoning Tasks
papers.abstract: Large reasoning models (LRMs) that leverage test-time computation achieve strong performance on mathematical and scientific benchmarks and are increasingly deployed in real-world applications. However, their ability to perform \textit{everyday logical reasoning}, which often departs from textbook formal logic, remains underexplored. In this work, we systematically evaluate how well reasoning models align with everyday reasoning patterns by introducing a benchmark based on linguistic and pragmatic reasoning phenomena. We also compare reasoning models with non-reasoning models under controlled prompting conditions. We find that, in many cases, (1) reasoning models show degraded performance in everyday reasoning when such reasoning deviates from formal logical rules, (2) some non-reasoning models with chain-of-thought prompting outperform comparable reasoning models in everyday reasoning, and (3) prompting with additional instructions provides limited control over reasoning behavior. These findings suggest that current reasoning models do not reliably capture everyday reasoning and point to limitations in post-training, motivating improved training objectives and evaluation across diverse forms of reasoning.

papers.title: Don't Retrain, Remix: Adaptation of Web Agents using Mixture Hypernetworks
papers.abstract: The web is not static or uniform. Websites that serve the same purpose can look and navigate very differently. Even within a single site, successive redesigns can change how familiar features are presented and accessed. Humans adapt to this by recognizing familiar interaction patterns and reusing what they already know. We give web agents a similar ability with WebMix, a mixture hypernetwork that adapts them to unseen interfaces by composing previously trained low-rank adapters. WebMix begins with a bank of adapters trained on source interfaces. At deployment, a scout agent explores the target interface and summarizes its observations into a compact manual. A lightweight router uses this manual to predict mixing coefficients over the adapter bank, which combine the existing adapters into a new one for inference. Adapting to a new interface takes only a scouting run and a forward pass, without gradient updates on the target. With Qwen and Llama models, we evaluate domain transfer on TimeWarp and WebArena-Lite-v2, and version transfer on TimeWarp. In all three settings, WebMix matches or outperforms in-context learning and LoRA baselines, often matching the average success of specialists trained directly on those interfaces. On TimeWarp domain transfer, it gains about 8 percentage points on average over the best baseline with both models. These gains do not come at the cost of seen interfaces, where WebMix keeps its lead, and extend to version transfer. Adapting to a new interface can therefore rely on exploration and composition instead of retraining.

papers.title: Hardy-Sobolev-Maz'ya inequalities for $\boldsymbol{1<p<2}$
papers.abstract: We establish Hardy--Sobolev--Maz'ya inequalities in the subquadratic range $1<p<2$ for singularities supported on affine subspaces and for arbitrary domains. We first prove a Hardy--Sobolev--Maz'ya inequality for singularities supported on affine subspaces of arbitrary codimension $1\leq k<N$, showing that the deficit in the sharp Hardy inequality controls a suitable weighted Sobolev norm. Combining the same convexity estimate with the one-dimensional approach of Frank and Loss in [9], we also establish Hardy--Sobolev--Maz'ya inequalities on arbitrary domains with the mean distance to the boundary and thereby solve a problem posed in [9]. These results complete the previously unresolved subquadratic range $1<p<2$ and, together with the known results for $p\geq 2$, provide a unified Hardy--Sobolev--Maz'ya theory for all $1<p<N$ associated with plane singularities and general domains.

papers.title: When frequency domain classification is superior to spatial
papers.abstract: Modern image classification models largely rely on local characteristics and feature extraction for their predictions. This focused approach works well in the spatial domain, but reportedly falls short in the frequency domain, even though both representations contain the same information. This study demonstrates that the significant reduction in accuracy in the frequency domain stems from the lack of local features. Locally swapping data in the frequency domain significantly decreases its inverse spatial domain accuracy, even below that of the frequency domain; however, the frequency domain accuracy remains relatively constant. Moreover, the use of datasets containing global features in the spatial domain yields higher accuracy in the frequency domain. Using these results, a hybrid model is constructed, combining one model trained only in the frequency domain and another trained only in the spatial domain to achieve higher classification accuracy. The proposed visual geometry group (VGG) and vision transformer (ViT) architectures are trained on the ImageNet-100, WikiArt, DTD, FMD, PSVRT, and KTH-TIPS2-b datasets and evaluated.

papers.title: Goodness-of-Fit Tests via Kernel Density Estimation: Univariate and Multivariate Approaches
papers.abstract: This paper introduces goodness-of-fit tests based on leave-one-out kernel density estimation (KDE) for both univariate and multivariate data. The proposed test statistic takes the form of a log-likelihood ratio comparing a parametric null model with a nonparametric KDE-based estimator, where the leave-one-out construction removes the in-sample bias inherent in standard kernel density estimators. For univariate densities with bounded support, boundary bias is mitigated via reflection techniques. We establish consistency of the proposed tests and show that, under fixed alternatives, the normalized log-statistic converges to the Kullback--Leibler divergence between the true density and the closest parametric model under the null, providing an information-theoretic interpretation of the procedure. A parametric bootstrap is used for finite-sample calibration. Extensive simulation studies and real data applications demonstrate strong empirical performance across a range of univariate and multivariate settings, including heavy-tailed, skewed, and multimodal alternatives.

papers.title: HeRE: A Novel Benchmark for Hebrew Relation Extraction via LLM-Guided Denoising of Knowledge Graph Alignments
papers.abstract: While LLMs demonstrate strong capabilities in English Relation Extraction (RE) tasks, a significant gap remains in assessing their RE performance in low-resource languages, due to a lack of standardized benchmarks. Creating native, language-specific annotated RE benchmarks is expensive and requires human expertise, while relying on translation yields suboptimal, inaccurate datasets that introduce English-centric biases. To tackle this, we propose a scalable, language-agnostic methodology to create RE data by denoising naturally occurring yet noisy alignments of knowledge bases and corresponding texts. We define a proper alignment via a Natural Language Inference (NLI) task, where a relation triplet is entailed by an input text. We empirically assess five denoising strategies, and demonstrate that multilingual models outperform language-specific models in the few-shot LLM setting, while Hebrew-specific encoders remain competitive under NLI fine-tuning and are strongest in the label-free cross-training setting. We further find that prompting in the native language achieves performance on par with or slightly exceeding English prompts, confirming that the pipeline operates naturally in the target language. The best open-weights model, Gemma-4-31B-it (F1\,=\,0.915), matches the best API model, GPT-5.4 (0.921), and reaches F1\,=\,0.844 on a fully held-out, dual-annotated test set. Applying the optimized pipeline, we release HeRE: a novel, massive, 1.5-million-instance silver dataset for Hebrew RE, designed to support data-intensive experimentation and model fine-tuning. HeRE bridges a critical gap in standard Hebrew RE evaluation, while providing the NLP community with a reproducible, language-agnostic pipeline for RE dataset construction in other low-resource settings.

papers.title: On the SPOT: Enhancing Speculative Decoding for Diffusion Language Models via Commit-Order Prediction
papers.abstract: Diffusion language models (DLMs) promise parallel text generation, but in practice face an unresolved speed-quality trade-off. Exact decoding fills in only one masked position per model pass, while faster multi-token decoding schemes are lossy. Speculative decoding is the standard lossless acceleration for autoregressive models. However, it does not transfer directly to DLMs, which must choose both what to generate and where. We show that this order is the missing piece: the model's own predictions from the previous pass already give the right token at over $90\%$ of positions, but not which position comes next. We introduce Speculating Positions Order Trajectory (SPOT), a 0.62M-parameter model that reads only the target's output distributions, predicts this order and proposes a tree of candidate continuations, which the target verifies in a single pass by state equality. Coupled-noise match, which shares Gumbel noise between drafter and target, keeps this verification exact at any temperature. This approach also inspired us to introduce SPOT-Sets for dynamic threshold decoding, where a pass commits several positions: SPOT-Sets drafts whole commit sets together with their tokens. Our comprehensive experiments show that SPOT cuts target passes by up to $6.8\times$ and reaches up to $3.4\times$ the throughput of standard decoding on SDAR-8B, matching or beating the calibrated and training-free drafting baselines in every task and budget at $T=0$ and $T=1$. In addition, we show that SPOT's learned drafter transfers across models, demonstrating successful transfer across six different DLMs; with a light calibration, the SPOT-Sets drafter transfers as well. On top of dynamic threshold decoding, SPOT-Sets improves the throughput of SDAR-8B by 59% on average over the threshold decoder alone. Project page: https://eliezer318.github.io/SPOT-dLLM/

papers.title: SIEVE: A Parameterized GitHub Corpus Builder for Software Engineering Research
papers.abstract: Software engineering research increasingly relies on large, richly annotated corpora of real-world code. Still, researchers typically assemble these with ad-hoc scripts or static, pre-built datasets that offer no control over corpus composition. This leaves a gap for a reusable tool that goes below the repository level and builds annotated, function- and class-level code corpora under researcher-specified criteria. We present SIEVE (Software Ingestion & Extraction for Verifiable Evaluation), an open-source, parameterized GitHub corpus builder that, unlike repository-level mining tools, works at code granularity: it locates individual functions, methods, and classes in repositories and extracts them as records, giving direct control over corpus construction based on several criteria, including widely used programming languages (Python, Java, JavaScript, C++), repository quality, and creation date. To support software engineering research and LLM evaluation on real-world code, SIEVE extracts CodeSearchNet- and OpenClassGen-compatible records, each annotated with 22 structural metrics and AST-derived features, and optionally with a CodeBERT-based P(AI-generated) score (F1=0.9478, AUROC=0.9902), alongside the third-party dependencies declared in each repository's package manifest. These annotations enable researchers to conduct structural analyses, investigate code dependencies, assess AI-generated code, and construct customized benchmarks for evaluating LLMs, including under temporal constraints. A manual validation of 400 records in four languages and two granularities shows 100% accuracy in code metrics and import detection, 99.0% in source completeness, and 99.5% in metadata accuracy. SIEVE is publicly available with a live demo at https://mrahman2025-sieve.hf.space.

papers.title: Cultural (In)Competence: Investigating Culture-Specific Stereotype Detection Capabilities of LLMs
papers.abstract: Stereotypes are subjective constructs that are mediated by the cultural context in which they are viewed. Successfully modeling them thus also requires cultural competence. When using large language models (LLMs) for stereotype-related tasks, such as their detection, it is therefore crucial that models can access relevant cultural knowledge and adjust responses accordingly. Since LLMs have shown disparities in what cultural knowledge is available to them, their capacity regarding stereotypes may also be disparate across languages and cultural contexts (e.g., for non-English languages or for non-US contexts). In this paper, we systematically investigate the effectiveness of LLMs for culture-specific stereotype detection across three factors: (1) the prompting language, (2) the instruction tuning language, and (3) the fine-tuning dataset size. We conduct experiments for US, Dutch, and Chinese cultural contexts. Our results suggest that LLMs do not reliably account for cultural contexts and overpredict the presence of stereotypes. Non-English prompts seem to improve consideration of cultural context and thus lead to more effective predictions. Moreover, we find that additional instruction tuning reduces false-positive rates and that training data size moderates detection effectiveness non-monotonically.

papers.title: An improved randomized algorithm for finding sinks of Acyclic Unique Sink Orientations of the binary hypercube
papers.abstract: Acyclic Unique Sink Orientations (AUSOs) of the binary hypercube form an elegant abstraction of various optimization problems, ranging from linear programs whose feasibility region is a combinatorial hypercube, to 2-player turn-based stochastic games (2TBSGs) in which one of the players has two actions from each one of its states. The currently fastest known randomized algorithm for finding the sink of such AUSOs is the Random-Facet algorithm of Kalai (STOC 1992), and of Matoušek, Sharir and Welzl (SoCG 1992), adapted to the binary hypercube by Gärtner (RSA 2002). The expected number of vertex queries made by the algorithm is at most $e^{2\sqrt{n}}$, where $n$ is the dimension of the cube. We design an improved randomized sink-finding algorithm that performs an expected number of only $e^{\sqrt{(2+o(1))n}}$ queries. This is the first improved bound for the problem in over two decades. The improved algorithm is obtained by adapting improved versions of the Random-Facet algorithm for solving general linear programs, and LP-type problems, developed by Kalai (STOC 1992), Gärtner (FOCS 1992), and by Hansen and Zwick (STOC 2015). The improved bound is not implied by these much more general algorithms. A key feature of the improved algorithm and its analysis is its simplicity. The structure of binary AUSOs enables a simpler description and a much simpler analysis of the adapted algorithm. In particular, the recurrence relations bounding the complexity of the algorithm depend on only one variable, and not two, and they can be solved using fairly straightforward techniques.

papers.title: Combining Rubin and Roman photometry and its implications for photometric redshift estimation
papers.abstract: We perform a joint Roman--Rubin photometry analysis using the LSST Science Pipelines (LSP) on simulated images, by using the Roman F158 band as the reference band and applying forced photometry on the other bands. We find that the LSP CModel photometry for Roman bands is on average unbiased, but with a bright-end systematic uncertainty floor of 7-8%. The pgauss photometry as part of the Metadetection weak-lensing shape measurement pipeline also exhibits a similar floor despite a substantially different flux-bias behavior. However, this systematic uncertainty floor becomes negligible for the color residuals and both algorithms recover unbiased colors for Roman as well as Rubin. We also show that not accounting for correlated pixel noise in Roman IMCOM coadded images results in underestimation of flux errors by a factor of ~4. Based on the measured photometry, we build a machine-learning algorithm that maps the true galaxy properties to empirical flux errors, providing a convenient method to reproduce realistic photometry errors without having to rerun expensive image simulations and photometry pipelines. We apply this empirical error model to a new mock galaxy catalog with improved realism to investigate the impact of different survey depths and configurations on photometric redshift (photo-z) estimation performance. We find that 1) Rubin survey depth significantly impacts the photo-$z$ precision, 2) additional systematic uncertainties on photometry could significantly degrade the photo-z performance especially towards high redshifts, therefore eroding the Roman--Rubin synergy, and 3) Roman photometry becomes important above z~1.5 while adding Rubin photometry to that of Roman improves photo-z performance across all redshifts. Our results provide a foundation for understanding how realistic uncertainties in galaxy photometry may propagate into the Roman--Rubin synergy in photo-z analyses.
authors: Roman HLIS Cosmology Project Infrastructure Team

papers.title: A thermally and perturbatively stable classical spin model in two dimensions
papers.abstract: We show that the 2D classical spin model constructed in arXiv:2605.10943 hosts many metastable states at non-zero temperature which are stable to arbitrary Hamiltonian perturbations, providing the first such example. Our proof relies on a recursive application of the cluster expansion.

papers.title: CFC26: Building Evaluations for Deployment in Sonar-Based Fish Counting
papers.abstract: Accurate counts of fish populations are essential for monitoring ecosystems and making decisions for conservation, harvest limits, and river management. In many field deployments, these counts are obtained from sonar videos that experts must inspect manually, making large-scale monitoring slow, expensive, and difficult. Automated counting systems have been proposed as a scalable alternative, but so far this promise has been difficult to realize in deployment. Developing evaluations that better reflect real-world deployment conditions will help close this gap and drive improvements in counting performance in practice. To achieve this, we propose Caltech Fish Counting 2026 (CFC26), a new dataset with improved evaluation protocols that simulate deployment to seen and novel rivers, testing in-distribution and out-of-distribution performance. We expand the CFC22 dataset to eleven deployment locations across nine Pacific salmon river systems from Alaska to Northern California, capturing a broader geographical and ecological range of data. We additionally introduce two new evaluation metrics for counting, nMNE and nMANE, that mirror the operational workflow that experts use and help surface errors that frame-level detection metrics do not capture. Using these metrics, we reveal previously-concealed directional bias in upstream vs downstream counts, which would have direct and significant ecological implications if undetected. The dataset and code are publicly available on CaltechDATA and GitHub.

papers.title: Local Projected Controllability of Nonlocal Continuity Equations
papers.abstract: We formulate and study the problem of local projected controllability (LPC) for characteristic solutions of controlled nonlocal continuity (transport) equations on the space of probability measures over a separable Banach space. The task is motivated in particular by self-interacting models in machine learning, whose action can be represented as controlled dynamics of the probability distribution over input data, while the actual output is given by a finite-dimensional vector of features extracted from the terminal distribution by a possibly nonlinear observation map. Given a fixed finite family of velocity fields which may depend on the transported measure, we ask whether the reachable values of the observable vector fill a neighborhood of its reference value. Our approach is to lift the transport equation in the space of measures to an ordinary differential equation on a Banach space of maps. This representation makes it possible to employ the machinery of Lie brackets developed for Banach manifolds, while the resulting sufficient condition for LPC can be formulated directly on the space of measures.

papers.title: Beyond What Is Visible: Context-Aware Sentiment Across Online Communities Among Crisis Events
papers.abstract: Social media offers timely insight into disaster experiences, yet online communities may not represent those affected on the ground. Uneven participation can bias crisis information systems toward data-rich locations and obscure communities with fewer digital traces. We address this with an adaptive cross-community learning framework that combines text and aggregate mobility signals with socioeconomic and hazard-informed community representations, supplementing sparse local observations with evidence from structurally related cities. We evaluate the framework on the January 2025 Southern California wildfires and 2024 Hurricane Helene in Florida. The adaptive model achieves the highest F1-score in both cases (0.5923 and 0.7615), while augmentation has its strongest effect where original observations are limited. The framework also reveals finer cross-city community-level sentiment variation and stronger sentiment-mobility correspondence than text-only models, with relationships differing across disaster contexts. These findings support crisis systems that better account for context-dependent evidence and improve interpretation of underrepresented community signals.

papers.title: RTISSLAM-3D: Full 6-DoF SLAM With an In-Air 3D Imaging Sonar
papers.abstract: Echolocating bats navigate dense forests using sonar alone, and in-air 3D imaging sonars now capture the entire frontal hemisphere with every pulse. Sonar SLAM, however, has so far been planar: current systems estimate a 2D trajectory and discard the elevation information in the sonar images, an assumption that does not hold on rough and sloped terrain such as a forest floor. In this paper, we introduce RTISSLAM-3D, a novel 6-DoF SLAM system for a wheeled robot that carries an in-air 3D imaging sonar, an IMU and wheel encoders. A CFAR detector on the sphere reduces every sonar image to a sparse set of 3D detections, which we use for a 3D acoustic odometry that models the shape of the sonar beam, for place recognition with polar submap descriptors, and for the verification of loop closures by 3D registration, all combined in a 6-DoF pose graph with attitude factors. We evaluated RTISSLAM-3D on a 545m drive through a forest, with a 3D lidar SLAM as reference. The loop closures reduced the horizontal error of the acoustic odometry from 1.74m to 0.28m, with a height error of 0.12m, and 94.6% of the resulting 3D sonar map lies within 0.3 m of the lidar map.

papers.title: Generative AI Produces and Transmits Beauty Bias
papers.abstract: Societies reward people judged to be attractive by standards intertwined with gender and race. In this paper, we examine if and how generative AI may contribute to these dynamics. We audited 27 text-to-image generators released between 2022 and 2026 using simple prompts that never mention attractiveness or beauty, analyzing 51,300 generated faces and 160,196 photographs of real people across primary and supplementary comparisons. We used three automated measures and collected ratings from 550 human raters on a subset of images. Nearly all generators produced faces scoring above photographed faces under automated measures, and human raters judged the outputs of all 23 generators as significantly more attractive than photographed faces, even after correction for multiple comparisons. When focusing our analysis on gender, we find that 37% of female-prompted generated faces outscored the median professional fashion model. Across racial, ethnic, and national categories, groups associated with darker skin tones tended to receive lower attractiveness scores than groups associated with lighter skin tones. In a preregistered hiring simulation experiment (N = 570), exposure to AI-generated faces selected for high human-rated attractiveness lowered hireability and trustworthiness ratings and reduced interview advancement for an identical test set of candidates paired with photographs of real people; exposure to retouched photographs produced no such effect. Generative AI can reproduce racial hierarchies and gendered patterns of beauty and alter the context in which real people are judged.

papers.title: Hausdorff Matrices on the BMOA and Bloch spaces
papers.abstract: We determine the spectrum and Fredholm essential spectrum of Hausdorff operators $\mathcal{H}_μ$ on BMOA and the Bloch space $\mathscr{B}$, for suitable finite positive Borel measures $μ$ on $(0,1]$.

papers.title: Atmospheric Chemistry-Climate Modeling with an AI Foundation Model
papers.abstract: Atmospheric composition and chemistry-climate interactions are central to predicting future climate change. Yet simulating chemical and aerosol processes is typically the most expensive component of an atmospheric model and is often highly simplified or prescribed entirely. AI weather forecasting foundation models have shown skill rivalling process-based models and are increasingly fine-tuned for new atmospheric tasks. Here, we present the first foundation model to capture interactions between emissions, atmospheric composition, and radiation. We fine-tune the Aurora Earth system foundation model on simulations from the chemistry-climate model UKCA. Our model reproduces daily meteorology, composition, aerosol, and radiation fields of the coupled system with 23 of 27 predicted fields achieving $R^2$ above 0.85 in both the troposphere and stratosphere. It reproduces ozone, CO, and temperature with annual mean biases below 4% and the downwelling shortwave and longwave fluxes to within 6%. Our model remains stable in autoregressive simulation over 50 years while running ~$100\times$ faster than UKCA. By training on paired emissions scenarios, our model learns responses to perturbations by capturing tropospheric ozone's response to changes in NO and CO emissions and surface radiation's response to aerosol. We further show that incorporating MLS satellite ozone retrievals into training corrects biases in the underlying UKCA fields, reducing zonal mean ozone error against collocated observations by 23% between 250 and 20 hPa. Our approach does not suggest process-based modeling can be replaced but demonstrates that a foundation model can be adapted to respond to forcings and learn from observations at a relatively small computational cost.

papers.title: When Plans Change, Remember: Replanning-Guided Visual Memory for Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.abstract: Long-horizon, multi-stage Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies often require visual information that is no longer present in the current observation. Retaining the complete observation history is computationally expensive and highly redundant, motivating selective visual memory. We introduce RePlanMem-VLA (Replanning-Guided Keyframe Memory for VLA), which turns a policy's own plan revisions into an online memory-write signal. Under receding-horizon execution, consecutive action chunks predict some of the same future actions. RePlanMem-VLA treats unusually large disagreement between these temporally aligned predictions as evidence of a task-relevant event. We first compare 35 disagreement measures across single-task autoregressive decoder-only and Flow-Matching Transformers trained from scratch, then validate the selected signals on pretrained OpenVLA-OFT and $π_{0.5}$ policies over MIKASA-Robo-VLA tasks. The resulting detectors achieve ROC-AUC of 0.981-0.997. We then use the selected signals in RePlanMem-VLA to trigger updates to a bounded visual memory, with a robot-masked write filter suppressing redundant frames. In the evaluated memory-retention experiments, RePlanMem-VLA preserves task-relevant observations until the later decision point in 100% of episodes. Real-robot replay data further show that event selection and redundancy suppression extend beyond simulation. These results establish plan revision as a policy-internal signal for controlling what a VLA remembers. Website: https://vika787.github.io/RePlanMem/.

papers.title: The transition between order to disorder in the Seppäläinen-Johansson model
papers.abstract: We study the Seppäläinen-Johansson model of first-passage percolation along a region of the plane where it moves from an ordered to a disordered phase, represented by a 2nd order discontinuity in its limit shape function. The fluctuations in this transition region are of order one, and we determine that certain limiting statistics are described by Fredholm determinants and are closely related to the largest eigenvalue of the GUE.

papers.title: Modeling and Analysis of Dynamic Coupling Effects in a Free-Floating Space Manipulator
papers.abstract: Motion of a robotic manipulator mounted on a free-floating spacecraft induces base translation and rotation, creating a dynamic coupling that affects end-effector motion. This paper characterizes that coupling in a planar three-link space manipulator. Using momentum conservation, velocity mappings are developed between manipulator joints, the end effector, and the spacecraft base. Singular value decomposition is then used to examine coupling strength, directional anisotropy, and the orientation of the coupled motions. Numerical maps show that coupling strength is invariant to the first joint angle but depends strongly on the relative configuration of the remaining joints. Increasing the spacecraft base mass reduces joint-to-base and end-effector-to-base coupling, while its effect on the joint-to-end-effector mapping is smaller and more dependent on configuration. The translational end-effector-to-base mapping is highly anisotropic in some configurations: its base-velocity ellipse becomes increasingly flattened as the weak coupling mode approaches zero. The principal end-effector and base velocity directions also change their relative alignment across the configuration space, producing predominantly opposing responses in some regions and transverse or approximately codirectional responses in others. Together, these results provide a geometric description of how coupling magnitude and direction vary with manipulator configuration and spacecraft mass.

papers.title: Four colours are needed for closed-neighbourhood conflict-free colouring of all planar graphs
papers.abstract: A colouring of the vertices of a graph is conflict-free with respect to closed neighbourhoods if every closed neighbourhood contains a colour that appears on exactly one of its vertices. The colouring need not be proper. Every planar graph has such a colouring with four colours. Fabrici, Lužar, Rindošová and Soták conjectured that three colours always suffice. We disprove this conjecture. We give a simple gadget construction that turns every planar graph of chromatic number four into a planar graph with no such colouring with three colours. This also shows that it is NP-complete to decide whether three colours suffice for a planar graph. We also give a planar graph on $25$ vertices that needs four colours. Further, we give critical planar graphs on $25$ vertices with $52$ and with $51$ edges, an infinite family of plane triangulations that need four colours, and an infinite family of critical examples.

papers.title: Geometric rigidity principles for $\mathscr{A}$-free Young measures
papers.abstract: We study generalized Young measures generated by $\mathscr{A}$-free measures, $\mathscr{A}$ a constant-rank operator, in a compactification of the value space adapted to an energy. Given an $\mathscr{A}$-quasiconvex integrand $G$ of linear growth with coercive recession function $G^\infty$, the unit sphere at infinity is replaced by the indicatrix $\mathbb{S}_G=\{G^\infty=1\}$, which need be neither convex nor symmetric. The two compactifications are equivalent, but in the adapted one the equality cases of the Jensen inequalities characterizing $\mathscr{A}$-free Young measures become statements of convex geometry about $\mathbb{S}_G$. We prove the characterization in this setting, with a new streamlined proof of the inhomogenization step based on a dyadic martingale argument. We then show that if $\mathscr{A}$-free measures $μ_j\overset{*}{\rightharpoonup}μ$ and their $G$-energies converge, then at $|μ^s|$-almost every point the concentration-angle measure is supported on the smallest exposed face of $\overline{\mathrm{co}}(\mathbb{S}_G)$ containing the $G$-polar of $μ^s$; in particular, it never charges the set where $G^\infty$ differs from its convex envelope, which, by the automatic convexity of Kirchheim and Kristensen, does not meet the wave cone. The concentration on the singular part of $μ$ is elementary for every such sequence if and only if each point of the wave cone on $\mathbb{S}_G$ is an extreme point of $\overline{\mathrm{co}}(\mathbb{S}_G)$, as for the Euclidean norm underlying Reshetnyak's continuity theorem; on flat faces of $\mathbb{S}_G$, rigidity degrades from a point to a face. Finally, we prove a transfer principle for the convergence of energies of $\mathrm{BV}$ maps under Dirichlet boundary conditions.

papers.title: FRACTAL: A Self-Similar Multi-Agent Orchestration Architecture with Formal Communication, Convergence, and Depth Bounds
papers.abstract: We present FRACTAL, a self-similar multi-agent architecture for recursive goal decomposition, in which the same five-component organizational pattern -- Orchestrator, Ensemble, Knowledge Ledger, Decision Maker, Meta-Observer -- recurs at every level of a decomposition tree. We make four formal contributions: (1) a communication bound showing intra-node cost is linear in ensemble size and round count (O(kr)) under a two-phase blind-proposal/stress-test protocol, versus quadratic cost for free-form debate, with an explicit, stated assumption on fixed evaluator count; (2) a two-mode orchestration criterion separating generative and evaluative phases via a measurable diversity-saturation threshold; (3) a supermajority convergence guarantee with explicit probability bounds at stated agreement levels, and a formal depth bound under an operationalized goal-complexity measure; (4) a Bayesian inter-layer escalation mechanism unifying hysteresis and contract-breach signaling under one posterior update. We illustrate the architecture's execution qualitatively on a worked example and a multi-layer case study; we do not report quantitative performance claims in this paper, and we explicitly discuss the formal and inductive-bias limitations of the model, including an unimplemented but architecture-compatible direction toward bounded self-improvement. We use "fractal" as an architectural metaphor for self-similarity, not a measured mathematical property. Empirical validation of the architecture's comparative performance is left to future work.

papers.title: Evolutionary Informed Translation from Protein to Nucleic Acid Sequence
papers.abstract: The choice of nucleic acid sequence for a given protein strongly impacts function and is species-specific. Current protein-to-nucleic-acid translation models treat sequences in isolation, often over-favoring frequently used codons. To generate more natural nucleic acid sequences, we introduce PINATA (Phylogenetically Informed protein to Nucleic Acid Translation with sequence Alignment), a model that leverages sequences from related species encoded in multiple sequence alignments (MSAs) to guide prediction. Our architecture leverages evolutionary context and learns species-and protein specific context to make biologically-informed predictions. Evaluated across 61,934 gene trees and 882 species, PINATA generates sequences that mirror the naturally-occurring sequence substantially better than existing language models. PINATA leverages MSA data to improve exact native codon recovery by 17.95 percentage points over existing language models, effectively preserves natural rare-codon nuances, and more closely matches native sequence properties. PINATA maintains strong predictive performance even with limited evolutionary data. While previous methods largely treated sequences from different species in isolation, our method leverages the evolutionary relationships between nucleic acids and proteins across species to create a more biologically-informed translation. We demonstrate that leveraging rich evolutionary data through an biologically-designed method strongly aids in translating protein sequences to nucleic acid sequences across species. We will make data and code publicly available upon publication.

papers.title: Micro-Localization: High-Precision Mobile Robot Localization Using Microscopic Ground Texture
papers.abstract: We demonstrate high-precision global localization using natural ground texture viewed through microscope optics, achieving localization in the tens-of-micrometers regime. For the planar ground texture localization problem considered here, we relate optical magnification and image-space localization uncertainty to physical localization precision. Leveraging this relationship, we then develop a microscope-based localization system that addresses the calibration, camera-modeling, and focus challenges introduced by high-magnification imaging. We evaluate this system across several surface textures using a calibrated precision gantry. Across 1,007 held-out queries per surface, the system localizes every query and achieves translation RMSEs of 28$-$73 $μ$m. Independent photometric registration agrees with the feature-based localization estimates to within approximately 9 $μ$m RMSE. We further demonstrate localization on a low-cost mobile robot using the gantry-collected maps, and also show that the system can resolve micrometer-scale displacement caused by thermal expansion. These results show that microscopic natural surface texture can bring mobile localization into a precision regime typically associated with fixed positioning systems.

papers.title: Deterministic Bounds on Accuracy and Stability of Metric-Space Regression and Classification
papers.abstract: Data-driven approaches often face ambiguity in datasets due to sensor or target noise, insufficient information, and noise in the input data. While best-fit machine learning methods can accommodate such noise through uncertainty estimates, they are prone to overfitting and it is challenging to quantify ambiguity of the relation between inputs and targets. We introduce a geometric framework that quantifies this ambiguity through the average kernel size, computed with data-dependent, i.e. model-independent, feasible sets derived from worst-case input and target noise. The framework provides computable, deterministic, non-asymptotic bounds on the best achievable empirical error and accuracy for a finite, constructed dataset, independent of the predictive model class, and applies to regression and classification with pseudo-metric input spaces and metric target spaces. The ambiguity of the input-target relation implies three consequences: an empirical error floor, an accuracy-stability trade-off, and, under standard probabilistic assumptions, a strictly positive distribution-training error gap when training below the accuracy bounds. Under standard Borel assumptions for Euclidean norms, the distributional analogue of the average kernel size is related to Bayes risk as it reduces to the optimal distribution root-mean-squared error times the square root of two. Experiments spanning tabular regression, image regression and classification datasets yield nontrivial bounds on the best achievable empirical error and accuracy on a constructed dataset, alongside descriptive comparisons with model performance on the original datasets. The bounds provide a computable, model-independent reference scale on the constructed dataset and comparisons with model performance on the original dataset are descriptive.

papers.title: Coverage Cliffs in Off-Policy Quantile Certification
papers.abstract: We study when logged contextual-bandit data can certify an upper tail quantile for a policy selected from the same sample. We construct a PAC-Bayes Bernstein lower-confidence envelope for the target cumulative distribution function (CDF), simultaneous over a predeclared threshold grid and all data-dependent posteriors. The resulting procedure, TailCert, uses the envelope's first crossing of level p to return an atom-safe upper confidence bound on the selected posterior's pooled p-quantile (or inconclusive). It can also be used to select a policy under a certified tail constraint. The concentration ingredients are standard; the main theoretical contribution is a matched finite-class certification boundary comparing full logs with their joint weighted CDF indicators at a fixed threshold. On an explicit rare-action class, the required sample size grows linearly with the overlap factor W, logarithmically with policy-search and confidence complexity, and quadratically with the inverse CDF safety margin; the upper and lower bounds agree up to constants in the stated regime. On this class, the CDF reduction hides which actions exceeded the budget; retaining action counts restores the full-log rate. Simulations verify the predicted search-complexity shift, winner's-curse failure of naive reuse, and the power cost of splitting.

papers.title: Seeing Seizures: A Large-Scale Empirical Study of Video and EEG Deep Learning for Automated Rodent Seizure Detection and Severity Grading
papers.abstract: Manual annotation of synchronized video and EEG recordings is a bottleneck in preclinical seizure research. We present an empirical study of seizure detection and behavioral severity grading using 24,131 paired clips from 601 sessions across 20 rats in a soman-induced epilepsy model. Ten video architectures and seven single-channel EEG models are evaluated independently on binary detection and three- and five-class severity tasks. In the session-exclusive reference comparison, R(2+1)D-18 and GRU achieve detection macro-F1 scores of 0.968 and 0.974, respectively; for five-class grading, the corresponding scores are 0.657 and 0.560. Subject-exclusive evaluation reduces five-class macro-F1 to 0.475 for video and 0.404 for EEG, highlighting the difficulty of grading unseen animals. Temporal-sampling experiments demonstrate the value of multiple frames, while detection performance varies relatively little across the evaluated video architectures. A separate video-only binary-detection evaluation on RodEpil achieves a mean seizure-class F1 of 0.979 after uniform re-encoding to reduce identified class-correlated encoding cues. The study characterizes existing models for behavior-defined severity labels under the evaluated protocol, motivating further investigation of expert-assisted annotation workflows. Our code and github page is available here.

papers.title: Who Do Perspectivist Models Predict Well? Annotator Agreement, Sparsity, and Performance
papers.abstract: Successful completion of perspectivist natural language processing (NLP) annotation tasks requires algorithms to be aligned across diverse perspectives in order to predict how different humans will rate text. This work studies how the performance of such algorithms varies for annotators who behave differently than others, either by providing annotations that diverge from others' responses or by providing fewer annotations altogether. To aid with characterizing model performance, we curate the largest collection to date of perspectivist NLP datasets with ordinal annotations. After evaluating multiple classes of perspectivist algorithms across each of the datasets, we model the relationship between individual annotator idiosyncrasy and algorithm performance. In general, we find that algorithms perform better on annotators who tend to agree with others, but that annotator response rate does not have a statistically significant positive correlation with algorithm performance.

papers.title: Repairing LLM-Generated Specifications with Deterministic Diagnosis
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as formalizers: given a reasoning problem expressed in natural language, they produce a formal specification that a symbolic solver can then solve, with guarantees relative to that specification. Many specifications are runnable yet semantically wrong, encoding incorrect constraints, domains, objectives, predicates, or goals, and solver-error feedback dries up once execution succeeds. Purely LLM-based diagnosis, lacking a formal ground truth, often fails to spot these errors, and its ungrounded critiques cause regressions in 11.8% of initially correct specifications in our experiments. We propose DRAGO, a repair framework that replaces this ungrounded critique with deterministic, formalism-specific diagnosis, and retains a rewrite only when the diagnosed error weight strictly decreases under a reference-free acceptance predicate. Across five benchmarks spanning logical reasoning (SMT-LIB2), constraint programming (MiniZinc), and planning (PDDL), DRAGO cuts regressions by nearly an order of magnitude, to 1.3%, while improving answer accuracy by 12.9 percentage points over zero-shot formalization and 8.7 percentage points over LLM-diagnostic repair, averaged across benchmarks. We also uncover two rendering defects in Planetarium that cause 50% (3,086 instances) of its floor-tile split to be inconsistent with the reference formalizations, and release a corrected split.

papers.title: Alignment of visual brain encoding models with individual perceptual similarity judgments
papers.abstract: Encoding models that predict brain activation responses to images have traditionally been trained to maximize accuracy when predicting observed brain data. However, their internal representations may not reflect individual human perception. In this work, we investigate whether we can fine-tune brain encoding models to better align their representations with individuals' similarity judgments. Using similarity judgments of 100 images from 8 participants in the Natural Scenes Dataset (NSD), we adapt a generic human similarity judgment model (DreamSim) separately for each participant to obtain personalized perceptual similarity models. These models are then used to obtain subject-specific similarity structure across images in their encoding model training sets. We fine-tune each participant's baseline encoder in two conditions, aligning its representations with either generic or personalized similarity judgments, with the same initialization and objective. We find that baseline brain encoders reflect within-subject perceptual similarity more strongly than measured fMRI responses and preserve intersubject correlations present in measured fMRI, but fail to reflect those of human perceptual similarity judgments. Fine-tuning with generic, population-level perceptual similarity information results in better alignment with human judgments than baseline encoders, but these models still fail to capture intersubject correlations of human judgments. However, fine-tuning with personalized perceptual similarity information results in models that are the most aligned with human perceptual similarity judgments and also reflect intersubject correlations of human judgments. Our framework provides an approach for bootstrapping human similarity judgment data into more individualized, human-aligned brain encoding models of vision.

papers.title: Embedding theorems for Herz-Type Sobolev spaces on domains
papers.abstract: In this paper, we further investigate the properties of Herz-type Sobolev spaces on domains, which unify and generalize the classical Sobolev spaces. In particular, we establish several Sobolev-type embedding theorems for these spaces. Moreover, by means of a suitable example, we show that some of the assumptions imposed on the parameters are optimal.

papers.title: Quantum Periods from TBA and Continued Fractions
papers.abstract: We consider quantum A-periods of local ${\mathbb P}^1 \times {\mathbb P}^1$, or equivalently the generating function of constant terms for powers of the Laurent polynomial $x + x^{-1} + y + y^{-1}$ where $x$ and $y$ are $q$-commuting variables. We derive a number of new representations for these rich combinatorial and algebraic objects. First, we find that the well-known TBA equation encodes not only the A-period itself but also higher diagonal modes of the corresponding noncommutative Laurent polynomials. Second, we obtain new formulas for the period in terms of continued fractions and related orthogonal polynomials, as well as a nontrivial explicit recursion allowing its efficient computation. Finally, we compute quantum corrections to the classical Picard-Fuchs equation, and observe that holonomicity of the classical period does not generalise to $q$-holonomicity of its quantum counterpart. Applications to random walks on the Cayley graph of the Heisenberg group, and related new approaches to more efficient generative AI systems, are outlined.

papers.title: DC-TORQ: Fast Assessment of Data Center-Induced Generator Torsional Oscillation Risk Quantification
papers.abstract: The periodic power demand of large data centers can introduce forced oscillations into the power system. When these oscillations contain frequency components near a turbine-generator torsional mode, they may excite sustained shaft torque oscillations with amplitudes exceeding the allowable cyclic torque limits. Characterizing the impact of data center power oscillations on generator shaft torque requires accounting for frequency-dependent network coupling among the data center, the transmission network, and the generators. Although electromagnetic transient (EMT) simulations can capture these interactions in detail, repeated simulations across excitation frequencies and load locations can be computationally demanding. This paper proposes an analytical framework for data center induced torsional oscillations that retains the coupled electrical and shaft dynamics. A detailed generator-network model is established, and closed-form transfer functions that map data center power perturbations to the torque in each shaft section are derived. Admissible shaft torque amplitudes are then translated into frequency-dependent limits on data center power oscillations. The proposed framework enables fast assessment of the shaft torque response while accounting for network dynamics and provides a quantitative screening criterion for candidate data center connection buses. The framework is validated on the IEEE benchmark model and applied to the IEEE 39-bus system.

papers.title: Computing S(X) for Ruled Surfaces Defined by Stable Bundles on Curves of Genus 2
papers.abstract: This paper discusses the algebra of symmetric tensors for ruled surfaces defined by rank 2 stable vector bundles on curves of genus 2. The algebra is computed for special bundles $E$ when $S^2 E$ is destabilized by a line bundle and when $S^3 E$ is destabilized by a bundle of rank 2. A strategy for computation is discussed in regards to the other special bundles $E$. This paper also discusses the generalization of these strategies to higher genus and gives a computation when $E$ is not stable and may be written as a direct sum of line bundles.

papers.title: Two-photon Doppler-free spectroscopy of the $6s^2\;^1S_0 \rightarrow 6s23s\;^1S_0$ Rydberg transition for quantum sensing in ytterbium
papers.abstract: Here we report atomic structure calculations and experimental observations of the two-photon $6s^2\;^1S_0 \rightarrow 6s23s\;^1S_0$ transition in Yb. The unique level structure of Yb places the $6s6p\;^1P_1$ state's energy at $\approx\!49.7\%$ of the ionization energy, which facilitates two-photon Doppler-free excitation of the $6s23s\;^1S_0$ Rydberg state from the $6s^2\;^1S_0$ ground state at a relatively low optical intensity. This $J= 0 \rightarrow J=0$ transition is immune to first-order Zeeman and electric quadrupole shifts, has reduced sensitivity to higher-order Zeeman shifts, and is further predicted to have relatively low sensitivity to density shifts. Using configuration interaction theory, we compute relevant properties of the $6s23s\;^1S_0$ Rydberg state for sensing, including the $C_6$ coefficient, dc polarizability, blackbody radiation (BBR) shift, and BBR depopulation rate. As a first experimental step, we demonstrate two-photon Doppler-free spectroscopy of the $6s^2\;^1S_0 \rightarrow 6s23s\;^1S_0$ transition. From our experimental spectra, we estimate the natural linewidth (lifetime) of the $6s23s\;^1S_0$ state to be 90 kHz (1.8 $μ$s). We believe this transition, or other $6s^2\;^1S_0 \rightarrow 6sns\;^1S_0$ transitions in Yb with $n\approx23$, may find use in a variety of sensing applications, potentially including a two-photon clock, electrometer, or BBR thermometer.

papers.title: Structure-Aware Spatial Kernels for Gaussian Process Distributed Port-Hamiltonian Systems
papers.abstract: Gaussian process distributed port-Hamiltonian systems (GP-dPHS) enable data-driven modeling of distributed dynamical systems while preserving their physical structure. However, standard stationary kernels can be inefficient for spatially heterogeneous systems because they neither exploit known input invariances nor reflect structured spatial dependencies. We address this limitation with a structure-aware kernel design that removes irrelevant state coordinates and decouples state and spatial dependencies through a tensor-product covariance. This modular construction allows qualitative knowledge of spatial heterogeneity to be incorporated by selecting an appropriate spatial kernel without requiring an analytical description of the underlying profile. Numerical experiments on a nonlinear string with periodic, smoothly varying, and semi-piecewise stiffness profiles demonstrate that structural decoupling consistently improves reconstruction accuracy, while profile-matched spatial kernels yield substantially larger gains in force-field and trajectory reconstruction.

papers.title: Embodiment-Classifier Guidance: Transferring Frozen VLAs Across Robot Dynamics without Demonstrations
papers.abstract: Flow-based policies such as $π_0$ are trained on a fixed set of embodiments, and transferring them to new ones is an open problem. To adapt a frozen $π_0$ to a new embodiment without additional demonstrations or parameter updates, we train a lightweight embodiment classifier to distinguish successful action chunks on the source body from those on the target body, using a few calibration tasks. On transfer tasks that $π_0$ saw on its source body but the classifier was never trained on, we nudge each denoising step of $π_0$ with the classifier's gradient, which estimates the direction from the distribution of successful actions on the source body toward that on the target body. On the LIBERO simulation benchmark with four modified controllers, embodiment-classifier guidance raises $π_0$'s average success on the target bodies from 72% to 80% across 12 suite-controller pairs, with a 31% relative reduction in failures (11 of 12 gain; 5 significant after Holm correction). In simulation, guidance is data-efficient, needing few target-body rollouts per task, which makes it promising for sim-to-real transfer, where rollouts are costly. Guidance is mixed on weak wrists and harmful on a locked wrist, when the classifier lacks data or favors infeasible motions. Collecting more target-body data with guided $π_0$ can fill such gaps: on one weak-wrist arm, guided $π_0$ solved a task on which unguided $π_0$ had zero successes in the original data, and retraining the classifier on the guided successes raised success from 52.5% to 70.7%.

papers.title: A Bayesian hierarchical model for preferentially sampled spatial extremes data: an application to air quality
papers.abstract: The National Ambient Air Quality Standards (NAAQS) establish concentration limits for criteria pollutants in order to safeguard public health and the environment. For some NAAQS, the standard refers to thresholds for either high percentiles or maxima. Identifying regions where regulatory thresholds are exceeded involves using geostatistical models, often formulated under the implicit assumption that observations arise from locations randomly sampled in the spatial domain. However, this does not hold for air pollution monitors as they are often preferentially placed in areas with elevated extreme concentration levels. Using the yearly maximum concentration of PM2.5 as a case study, we investigate whether preferential sampling affects inference and prediction for spatial extremes. To this goal, we propose a Bayesian hierarchical model that accounts for preferential sampling by introducing a shared latent, spatial process that informs both the median of the blended Generalized Extreme Value (bGEV) distribution and the probability that a site is selected to be a sampling location. Application of the proposed model to simulated data reveals that, not accounting for preferential sampling, results in systematic biases in parameters estimates, whereas application to observations of yearly maxima PM2.5 concentrations in California between 2017 and 2024 shows that not accounting for preferential sampling can significantly alter conclusions about exceedance regions.

papers.title: Model-as-a-Trojan: Self-Activating Covert DNS Exfiltration Baked Into the Weights of an LLM Agent
papers.abstract: Open-weight models are downloaded from public hubs and run inside agent harnesses that grant them tools, most powerfully, a shell, under the assumption that a sandbox contains whatever the model might do. This paper demonstrates that the assumption has a blind spot: the weights themselves can be the malware, and the sandbox's last open door, DNS, is enough. We fine-tune an open-weight LLM so that a single covert behavior lives in its parameters: on the first turn of every conversation, whenever the model infers from its context that a shell tool is available, it emits one self-contained command that reads a secret from the runtime environment, base32-encodes it, chunks it, and exfiltrates it as DNS queries toward an attacker-controlled authoritative name server. It then answers the user normally and never mentions, or repeats, the act. Because the channel is DNS, the attack completes from inside a container with no internet egress beyond name resolution - measured payload-level and model-level behind an egress firewall that drops every non-DNS packet, with the secret reconstructed from the gateway resolver's query log. Because the behavior lives in the weights, prompting is the only off-switch a victim has, and it is unreliable: the implant fires in 20/20 of adversarial suppression trials, deflects direct interrogation without disclosing the sequence, and sweeps a 45-cell sandbox-fault matrix across five tool-calling formats - plus a fresh post-training canary, persona-only and absent system prompts, and an egress-locked topology - with zero leaks and zero repeat fires. Every training trajectory is execution-verified in a real container, and every claimed exfiltration is proven resolver-side: we reconstruct the secret from the authoritative resolver's query log alone.

papers.title: MemLLM: End-to-end In-Storage Acceleration of On-device Retrieval-Augmented Generation using Precomputed KV Caches
papers.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) on edge devices enables personalized large language model (LLM) inference while preserving privacy. However, RAG's inherent length asymmetry makes the prefill phase the dominant bottleneck. While precomputing the KV caches offline alleviates the prefill cost on server systems, the multi-gigabyte caches over the narrow interconnect create a severe I/O wall for on-device systems. To mitigate this, we propose MemLLM, an end-to-end in-storage processing (ISP) architecture that executes the complete attention pipeline based on precomputed KV caches within the SSD.
